title: Kolkata's Floating Hotel Has a Railway Track Running Through It
excerpt: Polo Floatel Kolkata, India's only floating luxury hotel, has a working railway crossing on its grounds where trains pass within metres of guests — rooms run ₹4,000 to ₹6,000 a night.
body:
• A viral video has drawn attention to Polo Floatel Kolkata, where a working railway track runs through the hotel's landscaped grounds and trains pass within metres of guests.
  • The property is India's first and only floating luxury hotel, permanently moored on the Hooghly River in the heart of Kolkata.
  • Room rates typically range between ₹4,000 and ₹6,000, depending on season and availability.
  • The hotel sits 35 minutes from Kolkata Airport and 10 minutes from Howrah Railway Station, with Eden Gardens five minutes away.

A Crossing With Room Service

Most hotel lobbies offer a concierge desk. This one has a railroad crossing. A video shared on Instagram by user Krishan Goswami on June 29 has drawn fresh attention to a Kolkata property where a railway track cuts directly through the hotel premises — a yellow crossing sign, a designated crossing point and security personnel included — while trains rumble past guests strolling the manicured grounds.

The footage captures the surreal contrast that has made the property a social media curiosity: cobbled pathways, landscaped greenery and serene outdoor seating, with a functioning railway passage running through the middle of it all. Guests can be seen gathering around the crossing as trains pass, turning an ordinary stroll into an attraction in itself. The Hindustan Times, which first reported the viral video, noted that its reporting was based on user-generated content that it had not independently verified — a caveat worth keeping in mind, since the claim of a live track inside a hotel sounds almost too unusual to be real.

India's Only Floating Luxury Hotel

The property is Polo Floatel Kolkata, billed as India's first and only floating luxury hotel. It is permanently moored on the Hooghly River in central Kolkata, making it a curiosity twice over: a ship that functions as a full-service hotel, and a hotel with a railway line at its entrance.

The railway track appears to be the operational line running along the riverfront near the mooring — a reminder of how tightly Kolkata's colonial-era rail infrastructure is woven into the city's geography. The hotel's riverside position places it within easy reach of the city's landmarks: it is a 35-minute drive from Kolkata Airport, a 10-minute drive from Howrah Railway Station, and Eden Gardens — one of world cricket's most storied stadiums — is about five minutes away.

What a Stay Costs

For travellers tempted by the novelty, the pricing is firmly mid-market. Room rates at the Floatel depend on availability and season but generally fall between ₹4,000 and ₹6,000 per night — comparable to a standard business hotel in central Kolkata, with the river mooring and the railway spectacle thrown in. The property's rooms look out over the Hooghly, and the combination of waterfront setting and offbeat character has made it a favourite of travel content creators and domestic tourists looking for something beyond a standard city stay.

Why It Travels Well Abroad

For the diaspora, properties like this solve a familiar problem: what to show visiting friends and family — or to experience yourself on a return trip — that feels distinctly of a place. Kolkata's trams, its colonial architecture and its riverfront already give it one of India's most atmospheric urban identities; a floating hotel bisected by a live railway track is the kind of detail that turns a routine homecoming into a story. With Durga Puja season approaching and Kolkata at its festive peak, the timing of the video's resurgence is unlikely to hurt bookings.

What's Next

Social media virality is a double-edged sword for niche properties — the railway crossing is charming in a 30-second clip, but travellers booking a stay should check recent guest reviews for the practicalities of noise and train timings before committing. The Floatel's enduring appeal, though, rests on something sturdier than a viral moment: it remains the only hotel of its kind in India, floating on a river that has defined Kolkata for three centuries.
